claims.text: Rapid, low-temperature reduction of single-source precursors can produce multi-element, single-phase solid-solution nanoparticles.
The nanoparticles produced by the proposed baseline synthesis are near-equiatomic.
Limited free-atom or precursor mobility during formation favors formation of a random, single-phase multi-element alloy.
Increasing the number of atom types makes random-alloy formation more likely when free-atom mobility is limited.
Rapid low-temperature synthesis kinetically traps a high-entropy, disordered state.
Nanoparticles kinetically trapped during synthesis preserve a single-phase structure under catalytic and thermoelectric service temperatures extending as high as 1923 K.
Nanoparticles kinetically trapped during synthesis preserve chemical homogeneity under the specified high-temperature service conditions.
Low mobility during particle formation locks constituent elements in place and suppresses diffusion-driven segregation even during later high-temperature service.
A mild pre-quench annealing step increases atomic mobility and permits partial elemental rearrangement during formation.
Elemental rearrangement induced by mild pre-annealing promotes early-stage local segregation.
Early-stage elemental redistribution caused by pre-annealing makes the nanoparticles more susceptible to phase instability during subsequent service.
After high-temperature exposure, pre-annealed nanoparticles will exhibit more elemental segregation or phase separation than the unannealed control.
Segregation or phase separation in the pre-annealed nanoparticles will be accompanied by degraded catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The unannealed baseline nanoparticles are expected to remain single-phase and chemically homogeneous during high-temperature operation.
The proposed formation principle may extend to other low-temperature syntheses using similar solid, mixed precursors.
The atomic-mobility or annealing threshold for segregation depends on the alloy system and precursor chemistry.
XRD, TEM-EDX, or atom-probe tomography can be used to compare phase structure and elemental homogeneity between the annealed and unannealed batches.
